title: Advanced Helm: Hooks, Tests & Dependencies 🔧
description: Enhance your charts with lifecycle hooks, automated tests, and sub‑charts.

slides.title: Helm Lifecycle Hooks 🪝
slides.content:
# Run actions at specific points

Hooks execute one‑time operations during the release lifecycle:
- `pre-install`, `post-install`
- `pre-delete`, `post-delete`
- `pre-upgrade`, `post-upgrade`
- `pre-rollback`, `post-rollback`
- `test`

A hook is a regular Kubernetes object (Job, Pod) with an annotation:
```yaml
annotations:
  "helm.sh/hook": post-install,post-upgrade
  "helm.sh/hook-weight": "5"
  "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": before-hook-creation,hook-succeeded
```

Common uses: database migrations, certificate generation, cleanup.

slides.title: Hook Example: Database Migration
slides.codeSnippet:
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: {{ .Release.Name }}-db-migrate
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": post-upgrade
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: migrate
        image: myapp:{{ .Values.image.tag }}
        command: ["./migrate.sh"]

quizData.question: Which annotation defines a resource as a Helm hook?
quizData.explanation: `helm.sh/hook` tells Helm to treat the resource as a hook.

slides.title: Hook Weights and Deletion Policies ⚖️
slides.content:
## Ordering and cleanup

- **Hook weights** (`helm.sh/hook-weight`): hooks are executed in ascending weight order. Default weight is 0.
- **Delete policies** (`helm.sh/hook-delete-policy`):
  - `before-hook-creation`: delete previous hook before running a new one.
  - `hook-succeeded`: delete after successful run.
  - `hook-failed`: delete after failed run.

By default, hooks are not deleted; they remain for debugging.

slides.title: Chart Tests 🧪
slides.content:
## Validate your deployment

A chart test is a Pod (or other resource) with the annotation `"helm.sh/hook": test`. It runs when you execute:
```bash
helm test <release-name>
```

The test Pod should run a verification script and exit 0 on success. If the Pod fails (exit non‑zero), the test is considered failed.

Example: a Pod that curls the Service and checks the response.

slides.title: Test Resource Example
slides.codeSnippet:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: "{{ include "mychart.fullname" . }}-test-connection"
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": test
spec:
  containers:
    - name: wget
      image: busybox
      command: ['wget']
      args: ['{{ include "mychart.fullname" . }}:{{ .Values.service.port }}']
  restartPolicy: Never

quizData.question: How do you execute a chart's tests?
quizData.explanation: `helm test` runs all resources annotated with `test` hook.

slides.title: Managing Dependencies 🔗
slides.content:
## Sub‑charts and the `charts/` directory

You can include other charts as dependencies. Define them in `Chart.yaml`:
```yaml
dependencies:
  - name: mysql
    version: 9.x.x
    repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
    condition: mysql.enabled
    tags:
      - database
```

- `helm dependency update` downloads dependencies into `charts/`.
- `condition` and `tags` allow users to enable/disable sub‑charts via values.
- Values can be passed to sub‑charts using a `mysql:` key in your `values.yaml`.

slides.title: Library Charts 📚
slides.content:
## Reusable snippets only

A library chart (`type: library` in Chart.yaml) contains no Kubernetes resources, only template helpers (`_*.tpl` files). It cannot be installed directly; it’s meant to be imported by other charts.

Example use: a library of common labels, naming functions, or deployment patterns. Import it as a dependency and use its templates.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Use `helm lint` and `helm install --dry-run`

Always lint your chart (`helm lint ./mychart`) and dry‑run the installation (`helm install --dry-run --debug`) to catch template errors before deployment.
